title: Access to Justice in the Age of AI: Evidence from U.S. Federal Courts
author: Anand V. Shah · Joshua Y. Levy

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Effective help: Justice outcomes outrank lawyer supply
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s outcome-focused framing and materially strengthens it by distinguishing institutional access from professional productivity and by offering a conservative method for reducing termination bias in recent case-outcome measurement. The excerpt contributes methodological discipline rather than evidence that AI improves justice outcomes.
qs: Our approach (described in the methods, Section 2.3) is one (conservative) way to deal with the problem from measuring recent case outcomes.

Our setting differs in that the beneficiaries are not necessarily professional workers but individuals accessing a formal institution, and in that we don’t report the outcomes of an experiment with a particular model.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s proposition with large-scale federal-court evidence that cheaper AI-assisted document production is associated with increased self-representation and substantially greater docket activity. It supports the distinction between expanded court entry and effective justice, while showing that some resulting verification and processing burdens shift to courts; it does not establish worse remedies or directly assess users’ ability to verify AI output.
qs: First, the number of pro        se cases—or self-represented cases—is increasing dramatically, rising from a long-term        steady-state average of 11% to 16.8% in FY2025.
Moreover,        intra-case activity is up, with the total volume of docket entries per court generated        by pro se cases in their first 180 days up 158% from pre-AI means to 2025.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The paper accepts the cluster’s distinction between expanded legal-system access and improved access to justice, and materially extends it with large-scale federal evidence: self-representation and docket activity rose sharply, while resolution speed and apparent case quality did not improve. Its explicit causal caution and court-capacity implications reinforce the cluster’s emphasis on downstream, socio-technical outcomes rather than tool access alone.
qs: First, the national non-prisoner pro se filing share rose sharply from its approximately 11% historical steady state to 16.8% in fiscal year 2025, a gain that has no precedent in 25 years of administrative records.
Second, cases are not resolving any faster and analysis of case disposition suggests little change in the quality of cases brought by pro se litigants.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s task-specific, non-wholesale account and materially extends it with large-scale court evidence: post-AI growth concentrates in case types amenable to self-representation, while more complex work changes little. It also shows that cheaper production can increase system-wide docket activity, strengthening the case for selective deployment and operating-model redesign while remaining cautious about causality and outcomes.
qs: The simple category sees the pro se share rises sharply post-2022; the complex NOS pro se share barely moves.

It is that both sides are generating more docket activity at once, so the total burden a case places on the court during its first 180 days is rising on both sides of the bar, not just on the pro se side of it.

st.t: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: self-represented federal filings rose sharply in the GenAI era, yet cases did not resolve faster and disposition patterns showed little change in quality. Its account is associational rather than causally identified, consistent with the cluster’s caution against attributing the increase definitively to AI.
qs: First, the national non-prisoner pro se filing share rose sharply from its approximately 11% historical steady state to 16.8% in fiscal year 2025, a gain that has no precedent in 25 years of administrative records.
Second, cases are not resolving any faster and analysis of case disposition suggests little change in the quality of cases brought by pro se litigants.

st.t: Self-representation: Cheaper filings may shift institutional costs
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis: it documents a historically unusual rise in federal self-representation and docket activity after public GenAI release, while expressly disclaiming causal identification and finding no detectable change in resolution speed or outcome-based case quality. It therefore supports increased institutional burden without proving AI causation, improved litigant outcomes, or existing nationwide congestion.
qs: We do not claim to identify a causal effect of GPT-4 on pro se filing, only that the observed time series is difficult to rationalize without generative AI playing a role.
For example, between Sections 4.1 and 4.2 we note that the burden on courts has risen, though this has yet to generate sufficient congestion to have an effect on case resolution times.

kp.k: Federal self-representation increased sharply after longstanding stability
kp.d: The working paper reports that the national non-prisoner pro se filing share rose from a historical average of approximately 11% to 16.8% in FY2025. Annual pro se filings averaged 23,210 during FY2005–FY2022, compared with 27,370 in FY2023, 31,478 in FY2024 and 41,490 in FY2025. Pro se filings accounted for 18,280 of the roughly 31,170 additional civil cases relative to the pre-AI mean, or 59% of growth. Represented filings did not decline, making the findings consistent with new entry rather than demonstrating substitution away from lawyers.
qs: First, the national non-prisoner pro se filing share rose sharply from its approximately 11% historical steady state to 16.8% in fiscal year 2025, a gain that has no precedent in 25 years of administrative records.
Represented filings do not fall.
Pro se filings alone accounted for 18,280 of those additional cases.

kp.k: Evidence is descriptive, not causal identification
kp.d: The authors combine administrative records described as covering roughly 4.6 million non-prisoner federal civil cases in FY2005–FY2026 with 46 million PACER docket metadata entries. They exclude prisoner filings and organized mass-litigation events. Because capable LLMs became broadly available without a contemporaneous untreated comparison group, the attribution to AI rests on historical stability, timing, case-type differences and document detection rather than an identified causal effect.
qs: We do not claim to identify a causal effect of GPT-4 on pro se filing, only that the observed time series is difficult to rationalize without generative AI playing a role.
The only counterfactual available is the pre-AI time series in each unit, and so the identification argument throughout this paper is at best temporal stability

kp.k: Growth primarily reflects plaintiff-side entry across jurisdictions
kp.d: Plaintiff-side pro se cases increased from an annual average of 19,705 in FY2015–FY2022 to 39,167 in FY2025; defendant-side counts fell from 4,650 to 3,896, while both-sides cases rose from 775 to 1,081. The authors report that all but six states exceeded their own highest pre-AI annual filing count in FY2025, interpreting the broad geographic spread as difficult to reconcile with a purely local explanation.
qs: The post-AI rise in self-representation is a plaintiff story.
The increase in the total pro se count since FY2022 is therefore accounted for by plaintiff-side entry.
The rise in pro se cases is not driven by a handful of outlier districts.

kp.k: Document-production assistance matters most in self-help-compatible cases
kp.d: The authors argue that AI lowers the cost of drafting factual narratives and navigating filing requirements, with growth concentrated in civil rights, consumer credit and foreclosure cases rather than sustained-expertise categories such as patent infringement and securities fraud. Their main-text classification divides 86 Nature of Suit codes into 48 simple and 38 complex categories using the case-weighted median pre-AI pro se share. This is explicitly a revealed-preference proxy for self-help feasibility, not a direct measure of doctrinal complexity.
qs: We model AI as a productivity shock to the home production of legal documents.
It is not a literal measure of doctrinal complexity.

High pro se-share categories are categories in which self-help was already relatively attractive before AI, whether because the gain from counsel was small or because the effective price of counsel was large.

kp.k: AI may enable entrants and replace purchased representation
kp.d: The paper's theoretical model treats AI as reducing the effort cost and increasing the productivity of self-supplied legal work, thereby reducing the private value of hiring counsel. It allows both previously deterred litigants to enter and previously represented litigants to switch to self-representation. The authors additionally suggest that LLMs may reveal claims people did not know they had. These are proposed mechanisms; the observed filing trends do not separately identify their contributions.
qs: This model admits an increase in pro se cases being filed post-AI by both “entrants” new litigants entering the legal system and “switchers,” previously represented litigants choosing to file pro se.
A potential litigant who pre-AI did not know they had a cognizable claim now has access to a LLM that can advise them, and may file a claim they would not have known to file before.

kp.k: Docket activity indicates greater judicial processing demands
kp.d: Across 54 districts with full-feed PACER coverage and a 99.8% match rate, pro se docket entries per court during cases' first 180 days increased 64% on average over Q4 2022–Q2 2025 and 158% by 2025Q2 relative to pre-AI means. Entries per pro se case rose from 16.9 to 23.3, or 38%. The authors interpret docket entries as claims on court time, with both more cases and greater activity per case contributing to burden.
qs: By 2025Q2 (the most recent fully observable quarter at the 180-day horizon), the number of entries per court from pro se cases is up 158% relative to the pre-AI mean.
By 2025Q2, pro se entries per case reach 23.3, a 38% rise compared to the pre-AI mean of 16.9.
Each docket entry is a claim on the court’s time—a motion filed, a response submitted, an order entered, a hearing set.

kp.k: Represented litigation also shows increased activity
kp.d: Represented cases generated 22.5 docket entries per case in their first 180 days by 2025Q2, compared with 18.2 pre-AI, a 23% increase. The authors suggest that lawyers' own use of LLMs, including tools that free time for written submissions, could explain this intensive-margin pattern. They disclose a 2024Q4 metadata gap particularly affecting represented-case activity and caution that it does not affect filing or outcome data.
qs: Represented cases also generate more docket entries per case than they did before: 22.5 in 2025Q2 versus 18.2 pre-AI, a 23% rise in the first 180 days.
This can be explained by attorneys using LLMs too, suggesting LLMs are having an important intensive-margin effect for both groups as a general technology that lowers drafting costs.

kp.k: Case resolution and outcome composition remain broadly stable
kp.d: Using horizon-specific observation windows to address right-censoring, the authors find that FY2023–FY2025 pro se cases resolve at approximately the pre-COVID FY2015–FY2019 pace. Among classified terminations within 180 days, judicial dismissals increased from approximately 60% to 63%, settlements from roughly 20% to 23%, and pro se losses declined from 19% to 13%; unambiguous wins remained below 1%. They interpret the composition as showing little detectable change in case quality, despite increased activity and volumes; the outcome analysis is restricted to cases resolving within the observation window.
qs: Cases filed in FY2023–FY2025 resolve no faster or slower than cases filed in FY2015–FY2019.
The composition of outcomes appears broadly stable.
Smaller values of W retain filing cohorts closer to the right edge of the data set, but only identify outcomes among fast-resolving cases.

kp.k: Complaint detection provides qualified evidence of growing AI use
kp.d: The authors apply Pangram's commercial AI-text detector to 1,600 complaints sampled from CourtListener/RECAP: 200 per calendar year from 2019 through early 2026, including represented and pro se cases. The detector flagged 1 of 800 pre-period documents and 66 of 800 post-period documents. Annual rates rose from 1.0% in 2023 to 3.5% in 2024, 10.5% in 2025 and 18.0% in early 2026. RECAP disproportionately captures documents uploaded by attorneys, journalists and researchers, underrepresenting pro se text. The authors' suggested lower-bound interpretation depends on pro se litigants using AI more frequently than attorneys.
qs: The pre-AI period (2019–2022) yields 1 detection across 800 documents, a rate of 0.1%.
The post-AI period (2023–2026) yields 66 detections across 800 documents, a rate of 8.2%.
The rate rises monotonically from year to year: 1.0% in 2023, 3.5% in 2024, 10.5% in 2025, and 18.0% in early 2026.
If pro se litigants are using AI at a higher rate than attorneys, that suggests that our results are a lower bound for the true prevalence of AI-text in legal cases.

kp.k: Vermont illustrates AI drafting combined with lawyer verification
kp.d: The appendix describes immigration mandamus filings against USCIS in Vermont, where pro se filings rose from roughly 45 annually before 2022 to over 1,100 in FY2024. A December 2024 Reddit guide described Microsoft Copilot drafting followed by a $150 Fiverr lawyer review, illustrating a hybrid self-help pathway rather than wholly autonomous legal work. The authors characterize this as strategic forum shopping supported by online instructions and state that excluding Vermont leaves the national findings qualitatively unchanged.
qs: Step 2 describes hiring a Fiverr lawyer for $150 to review and polish the AI-generated draft.

The Reddit post suggests that applicants with no legal training use an LLM to generate an initial draft, pay a small amount for a lawyer to review it, and file the result in a strategically chosen venue.
We describe the phenomenon here and show that excluding Vermont from the sample leaves the paper’s results qualitatively unchanged.

kp.k: Access gains may create congestion and asymmetric litigation
kp.d: The authors predict that effects could be larger in state and municipal courts, which have lower entry barriers and handle over 90% of litigation in the cited account; this is not measured by their federal study. They also outline possible escalating written-submission competition and disproportionate pressure on government defendants whose response capacity may not scale with AI-assisted plaintiffs. These are prospective risks, while their observed federal duration measures do not yet show increased congestion.
qs: If generative AI is enabling self-representation in this demanding context, the effect in state and local courts is likely larger still.
The first is an arms race between private litigants.

The second is asymmetric litigation against institutional defendants, particularly the federal government and large administrative agencies that cannot easily scale their litigation capacity in response.

The courts are not yet visibly buckling under the load—case durations are stable and dispositions look familiar—but the volume of activity inside cases has risen sharply and shows no signs of stopping.

kp.k: Authors propose expanding adjudicative capacity and AI assistance
kp.d: The paper argues that congressional control over judgeships, lengthy judicial formation and what it describes as restrictions on AI opinion drafting constrain supply. It proposes relaxing judicial AI restrictions, routing simple cases to magistrates, lower courts or specialized triage, and potentially creating a new lower court using AI for the simplest cases. These are policy proposals, not evaluated interventions; the paper acknowledges that the options are not costless.
qs: One margin for this is to relax the rules that prohibit federal judges from using AI assistance, enabling a productivity response on the adjudication side analogous to the one AI has already produced on the filing side.
Another is to more aggressively route simple cases—the cases we show drive the bulk of the post-AI rise—to magistrate judges, lower courts, or specialized triage procedures.
These avenues are not mutually exclusive, and neither is costless.

kp.k: Lawyer displacement and market restructuring remain open questions
kp.d: The authors propose future lawyer-level research rather than report established employment effects. Possible trajectories include substitution in simpler matters, augmentation in complex litigation, AI-generated referrals to lawyers, and disproportionate gains for technically adept practitioners. They explicitly leave unresolved whether AI will promote consolidation around large firms or empower independent lawyers to handle more demanding work. Planned research also includes complaint quality, citation hallucination, document homogenization and distinguishing new litigants from repeat filers.
qs: If AI is substituting for legal professionals for “simple” cases, but labor-augmenting for the most “complex” cases (perhaps because these cases are less rote, or because litigation strategy becomes more important), then the constituents of the legal industry may benefit or lose differentially
Alternatively, perhaps AI tools empower independent practitioners to take on ever more complex cases and demanding clients
We do not take a stance on which effects will dominate or how the legal industry will respond to increasingly capable generative AI tools.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Shah and Levy argue that generative AI lowers the cost of self-representation, contributing to increased federal civil filings and docket activity without a visible change in case resolution times or disposition patterns. They predict possible congestion and heterogeneous legal-market effects, while declining to identify a causal effect or a dominant future market structure.
pts.d: The authors make several distinct claims. (1) AI supplies inexpensive case-specific guidance and passable legal documents, making court entry more feasible for non-lawyers. Non-prisoner pro se filings increased from a long-run share of approximately 11% to 16.8% in FY2025; annual counts reached 41,490 compared with a FY2005–FY2022 mean of 23,210. Pro se cases accounted for 59% of the increase in total civil filings relative to the pre-AI mean. The increase primarily involves self-represented plaintiffs, not defendants. (2) Gains concentrate in categories amenable to standardized factual narratives and document production, such as civil rights, consumer credit and foreclosure, rather than categories requiring sustained specialist expertise. Their model treats AI as improving household production of legal services, potentially inducing both new court entrants and formerly represented litigants to self-represent. Since represented filings do not fall, the evidence does not establish net replacement of lawyers. (3) Increased case volume and submissions within cases imply greater court burden: first-180-day pro se docket entries per court were 158% above the pre-AI mean by 2025Q2; entries per pro se case rose 38%, while represented-case entries rose 23%. The authors interpret the latter as consistent with lawyers also using AI or reallocating time saved elsewhere toward submissions. (4) They find no visible acceleration or slowdown in resolution and broadly stable disposition shares, which they interpret as little detectable change in case quality—not as demonstrated improvement in litigants’ chances of winning. (5) Detector results indicate increasing AI-generated text in complaints. (6) They expect effects and burden to be larger in state and municipal courts, but do not present results for those courts. (7) They describe possible future escalation of written submissions and asymmetric pressure on government defendants whose response capacity may not keep pace. (8) They anticipate changes in legal employment but leave competing possibilities open: substitution for lawyers on simple cases, augmentation on complex cases, increased referrals to lawyers, advantages for technically proficient practitioners, consolidation into large firms, or stronger independent practices. (9) They propose possible supply-side responses—AI assistance for judges, greater routing to magistrates or specialized triage, and potentially a new lower court using AI for simple-case triage—rather than reporting that these responses have occurred or proven effective.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source combines descriptive administrative time series, docket metadata, AI-text detection, a theoretical model and an illustrative immigration-filing case study. Its broader market and congestion predictions are conditional extrapolations, not measured outcomes.
pts.d: The paper describes an overall administrative universe of approximately 4.5–4.6 million non-prisoner federal civil cases spanning FY2005–FY2026, with an approximately 3.7-million-case duration/disposition sample. It uses AOUSC C-13 filing counts and the FJC Integrated Database, excludes prisoner cases and organized mass-litigation events, and matches 46 million PACER docket entries. Docket analysis covers 54 of 94 districts with full-feed access, a reported 99.8% match rate, and roughly 80% of non-prisoner pro se filings. Temporal evidence includes the long pre-AI stability, post-2022 divergence, broadly pervasive geographic growth, and concentration in high-baseline-pro-se case types. All but six states reportedly exceeded their earlier peak pro se filing count in FY2025. The simple/complex grouping uses pre-AI pro se shares as a revealed-preference proxy, with alternative percentile cutoffs used for robustness; it is not a direct measure of doctrinal complexity. Outcome analyses compare fixed observation horizons, principally 180 days. Judicial dismissals account for approximately 60% of classified pro se terminations pre-AI and 63% post-AI; settlements approximately 20% and 23%; unambiguous losses 19% and 13%; wins remain below 1%. These are disposition proxies for quality, not direct assessments of merits or settlement value. For document-level evidence, the authors apply Pangram to 200 sampled complaints or petitions per calendar year from 2019–2026 in CourtListener/RECAP. Detections are 1/800 in 2019–2022 and 66/800 in 2023–2026, with annual rates of 1.0%, 3.5%, 10.5% and 18.0% in 2023 through early 2026. This is detector classification, not independently verified authorship or a pro-se-specific adoption rate. The paper cites Imas and Jabarian’s detector evaluation and uses the pre-period to calibrate false positives on legal complaints. Appendix A offers a concrete but illustrative mechanism: a Reddit guide describes drafting an immigration mandamus filing with Microsoft Copilot and paying a Fiverr lawyer $150 to review it. Vermont pro se filings rose from roughly 45 annually to over 1,100 in FY2024; excluding Vermont leaves the national pattern qualitatively unchanged. The home-production model explains potential entry and substitution but does not estimate their respective magnitudes. GPT-4 bar-exam and LegalBench results are cited as capability context, not as proof of effects on filings. State-court burden, future arms races, agency queues and legal-industry restructuring remain predictions or hypotheses. Supply-side arguments invoke judgeship constraints and the authors’ assertions about judicial AI policies and attorney certification requirements.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Observed changes concern the period after ChatGPT and GPT-4 became widely available, principally FY2023–FY2025, with text-detection evidence extending into early 2026. Predictions extend into unspecified coming months and years and depend on adoption, task characteristics and institutional responses.
pts.d: The March 2026 working paper associates the filing break with widespread access to capable LLMs, using ChatGPT’s November 2022 release and GPT-4’s March 2023 release as temporal markers rather than isolated treatments. C-13 pro se shares were 11.6% in FY2022, 11.4% in FY2023, 14.5% in FY2024 and 16.8% in FY2025; the increase was therefore not an immediate upward jump in the share in FY2023. For docket activity, the post-AI comparison period is Q4 2022–Q2 2025, with the strongest changes appearing in 2025, which the authors suggest may reflect diffusion. The latest fully observable quarter for first-180-day docket measures is 2025Q2. Outcomes are observed through December 31, 2025, and comparisons require sufficient follow-up; disposition findings chiefly describe cases terminating within 180 days, not the eventual outcomes of all recent cases. Alternative windows are reported, but a 365-day window excludes 2025 filings. Duration comparisons use FY2015–FY2019 to avoid pandemic confounding. A localized 2024Q4 metadata gap particularly affects represented-case docket measures, not filings or outcomes. The text sample covers early rather than full-year 2026 and is drawn from an incomplete public archive disproportionately accessed by attorneys, journalists and researchers. Its proposed lower-bound interpretation holds only if pro se litigants use AI more frequently than attorneys. The authors explicitly lack a causal design and acknowledge that other shocks could contribute to observed patterns. Their simple-case mechanism depends on filing-stage work constituting a substantial portion of litigation costs; complex cases may still require discovery, strategic work and experts. Predictions of congestion or an arms race require continued growth in submissions without commensurate adjudicative capacity. The current findings do not show court durations increasing. Proposed changes to court organization or judicial AI use are contingent policy options, and the source does not give a date for implementation or quantify their effects.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied parties are non-prisoner federal civil litigants and district courts. The authors foresee consequences for access to justice, government defendants, lawyers and firms, while not establishing demographic benefits, net lawyer displacement or a particular market winner.
pts.d: Self-represented plaintiffs are the primary observed beneficiaries of lower document-production barriers: they may pursue claims they previously would not have filed, or substitute self-help for counsel. Plaintiff-side pro se counts rise from a FY2015–FY2022 mean of 19,705 to 39,167 in FY2025; defendant-side counts fall from 4,650 to 3,896, with a modest increase in cases where both sides are pro se. Individuals with civil-rights, consumer-credit, foreclosure and other template-amenable disputes are especially implicated. The study concerns access to a formal institution rather than enterprise legal-cost savings; however, it has no filer demographic data and does not demonstrate that the additional litigants are low-income or that their substantive outcomes improve. Lawyers and represented parties may also gain drafting productivity or reallocate saved time toward additional submissions, potentially increasing rather than reducing litigation activity. Courts, judges and staff face more matters and more docket activity without an observed change in resolution speed; the authors describe adjudicative capacity as tightly constrained. Federal agencies and other institutional defendants may face growing response obligations because plaintiffs’ filing costs fall faster than institutional litigation capacity expands. State and municipal courts, and users in family, traffic and business matters, are predicted to experience potentially greater pressure, but are outside the reported empirical analysis. Legal-profession effects remain ambiguous: practitioners handling simple cases could lose work, complex-case lawyers could be augmented, technically adept lawyers could gain disproportionately, and AI advice could generate demand for professional representation. Large firms might consolidate the market if only they can supply services beyond AI’s reach, or independent practitioners might compete for increasingly complex matters. Prospective lawyers and other legal professionals may consequently face changes in career opportunities. The authors make no determination of which group will ultimately gain or lose.
